items.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995
items.q: my daddy was out the house and I could see him going to work

ctx.x: And the music was, at that time. You see people had control over where you could go, where you could sit, but the one thing about that music was that it was the radio, the disc jockeys who played that music who were responsible for the music becoming what it was. And parents, unlike today with television I think and changed channels, they had no control over the radio dial, you see? And I’ve had many kids come to me and say they had to hide their radio, put the pillow over it, anything so the parents wouldn’t…

my daddy was out the house and I could see him going to work, I would switch the dial to a radio station that played a program “The Mail Bag.” My daddy didn’t want us to hear it in the house. But as soon as he was out, you know, that’s where we would turn it, to “The Mail Bag.” So radio was very very important in that particular time. The DJs, you’d get into town and you’d have to go in to these radio stations and talk, and a lot of times people would not buy tickets because you bought tickets at the door. There…
And that was done by a guy called a “front man?”
